extracted.intended_audience: researchers and advanced students in philosophy of mathematics, automated theorem proving, and mathematical practice interested in formal accounts of proof planning
extracted.subtask_description: Formal account of how plans for mathematical proof activities are constructed and executed: nodes are proving intentions (types 'to show' and 'to infer'), transformed step-by-step by practical reasoning and mathematical methods; includes schema-level characterizations, directionality, resolution expertise, and modular presentation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving intentions as plan atoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Proving intentions—of types 'to show' and 'to infer'—constitute the building blocks or atoms of plans for proof activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each node of a plan is a proving intention; plans are constructed by transforming these intentions into more specific intentions arranged in subplans. Use the compact notation for premisses P1, ..., Pn and conclusion C as the premisses and conclusion of a proving intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical reasoning takes as input a given proving intention in the agent's plan and yields as output one or several more specific proving intentions arranged in a subplan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical reasoning is the central step-by-step process by which plans are constructed: each construction step of a plan results from an instance of practical reasoning. It can be explicit in written proofs (as in Fraleigh's proof) or left implicit (requiring listing implicit 'to infer' steps in schemas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical method (schema form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical method is a rule that transforms a proving intention into one or several other proving intentions arranged in a subplan, often characterized by a schema specifying its input-to-output transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General schema form: 'To show C, from [P1,...,Pn]: 1. Show/Infer C1, ... k. Show/Infer Ck, from [P1,1,...], ... from [Pk,1,...]' (placeholders Cs and Ps represent propositions). The output of a method is a subplan (tree); exposition here restricts to subplans of depth one but methods can yield deeper subplans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace term by its definition (method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Method that replaces a term by its definition inside the proposition to be shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schema: 'To show X[Φ], from [P1,...,Pn]: 1. Show X[ΦDef/Φ], 2. Infer X[Φ], from [P1,...,Pn], from X[ΦDef/Φ] and ΦDef.' Φ is a term placeholder, ΦDef its definition; include the usually implicit 'to infer' deductive step when completing the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set equality via mutual inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Show A = B by proving A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A and then inferring equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schema: 'To show A = B, from [P1,...,Pn]: 1. Show A ⊆ B, 2. Show B ⊆ A, 3. Infer A = B, from [P1,...,Pn], from A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.' Order may be immaterial informally, but the formal method yields an ordered subplan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary logical/set-theoretic methods (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic methods such as conjunction introduction and modus ponens transform goals into subgoals following logical rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: conjunction introduction — 'To show X ∧ Y, from [P1,...,Pn]: 1. Show X, 2. Show Y, 3. Infer X ∧ Y.' Modus ponens — 'To show C, from [P1,...,Pn,X,X→Y]: 1. Infer Y, 2. Show C, from X and X→Y.' These are widely applicable across mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical induction (context-restricted method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is a mathematical method that applies to universal claims over natural numbers and has a specific input/output schema.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schema: 'To show ∀n H(n), from [P1,...,Pn]: 1. Show H(0), 2. Show ∀p(H(p)→H(p+1)), 3. Infer ∀n H(n).' Note: such methods have restricted domains of applicability (e.g., number theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific methods (e.g., isomorphism test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some methods apply only within specific mathematical domains (e.g., group theory) and have specialized schemas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Fraleigh): to show φ:G→G' is an isomorphism: 1. Show φ is a homomorphism, 2. Show Ker(φ)={e}, 3. Show φ maps G onto G', 4. Infer isomorphism. Such methods rely on domain theorems and definitions (e.g., theorem T, definition of isomorphism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of generality of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical methods come at different levels of generality in terms of their range of application: some methods are widely applicable, others are domain-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical/set-theoretical methods (conjunction, modus ponens) are broadly applicable; induction or isomorphism tests are restricted. Consider applicability when selecting methods in planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directionality of methods: forward, backward, mixed
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical method proceeds forward if outputs differ from input only in hypotheses; backward if outputs differ only in conclusion; mixed if neither holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: forward methods extend hypotheses (move toward conclusion by strengthening premises); backward methods transform the conclusion into simpler goals. Typical human proofs mix forward and backward steps; automated systems also use this terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution expertise (method selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolution expertise is the epistemic process that takes a proving intention and yields the mathematical method the agent judges to have the best chance of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When multiple methods apply, the agent need not consider every method: (i) exclude methods whose input schema doesn't match; (ii) exclude methods known not to succeed. The paper does not specify decision mechanisms (this touches on proof-discovery and tactic selection research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple applicable methods and choice necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Several different mathematical methods can often be applied to the same proving intention; a choice must be made which method to apply before transforming the intention into a subplan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: goals of the form ∀n P(n) might admit induction or various case-splitting strategies. This motivates the need for resolution expertise and tactic-selection mechanisms in provers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plans for proof activities (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An agent's plan for a proof activity is an ordered tree such that (1) each node is a proving intention, (2) the root is the proving intention corresponding to the theorem, and (3) each set of ordered children of a parent node is a subplan obtained from the parent by an instance of practical reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Execution of the plan realizes the proof activity as the sequence of deductive inferences (actions). The written mathematical proof is a report of this activity where the order of deductive steps corresponds to execution order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modular descriptions and modular presentations of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Modular descriptions: any subtree of a plan can be viewed as a module described by the proving intention at its root; modular presentations replace deductive steps inside modules by the module's root intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modular presentation encapsulates 'how' into a module and states only 'what' is shown at the module root. Benefits: increases comprehensibility, communicability, readability, and rigor (as argued via Leron and Lamport). There are multiple possible modular descriptions/presentations depending on omitted subtrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reasoning complexity: routine vs sophisticated
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical reasoning instances range from routine (applying standard methods) to sophisticated (trial-and-error, heuristic-driven strategy changes, auxiliary constructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Pólya's Carleman inequality proof: heuristics like 'apply an inequality where it is nearly sharp', introduction of auxiliary sequences (ci) to make AM-GM nearly sharp, trial-and-error and analysis of why attempts fail, backtracking and strategy refinement. Such higher forms go beyond simple schema application but still conform to stepwise plan construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit listing of implicit deductive steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Written proofs often omit implicit 'to infer' intentions/deductive steps; formal plans/schemas should include them to complete the subplan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnotes note that some 'to infer' intentions are left implicit by authors (e.g., Fraleigh); for formal plan representation, include these inferential intentions in the schema to account for completeness of the plan.
